60.2: whose body remains set into a brazen cauldron; and they ever cook it.
60.3: One foot, which is the right one, remained outside the cauldron.
60.4: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this body?'
60.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
60.6: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked man who, among the living, lustfully and improperly, went much out to married women;
60.7: and his whole body became sinful.
60.8: But that right foot, the frog and ant, snake and scorpion, and other noxious creatures ( khrafstars ) were much smitten and killed and destroyed.'

61.1: I also saw the souls of those wicked
61.2: who swallowed and voided, and again swallowed and voided.
61.3: And I asked thus: 'What souls are those of these?'
61.4: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
61.5: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked who, in the world, believed not in the spirit,
61.6: and they have been unthankful in the religion of the creator Ohrmazd.
61.7: they have been doubtful of the happiness which is in heaven, and the torment which is in hell, and about the reality of the resurrection of the dead and the future body.'

62.1: I also saw the soul of a woman
62.2: who ever gnashed her own bosom and breasts with an iron comb.
62.3: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this body, whose soul suffers so severe a punishment?'
62.4: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
62.5: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked woman who, in the world, despised her husband and master (or guardian,) and became and remained vile;
62.6: being also herself untrue to him, and acted improperly with other men.'

63.1: I also saw the soul of a woman
63.2: who ever licked a hot oven with her tongue,
63.3: and ever burnt her own hand under the oven.
63.4: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this body, whose soul suffers so severe a punishment?'
63.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
63.6: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked woman who, in the world, offered defiance to her own husband and master, and became abusive;
63.7: she also acted disobediently, and did not grant cohabitation at his desire;
63.8: and she stole property from her husband, and secretly formed a hoard for herself.'

64.1: I also saw the soul of a woman
64.2: who ever came and went crying and wailing;
64.3: upon her head also, ever came pelting hail;
64.4: and under foot, hot, molten brass ever streamed;
64.5: and she ever gashes her own head and face, with a knife.
64.6: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this body, when the soul ever suffers so severe a punishment?'
64.7: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
64.8: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked woman who, undutifully, became pregnant from other men,
64.9: and she effected the destruction of the infant. [i.e. abortion or infanticide]
64.10: Because of the pain and punishment, she fancies that she hears the cry of that infant, and she runs;
64.11: and such vehemence of running is occasioned, as of one who walks upon hot brass;
64.12: and she ever hears the cry of that infant, and gashes her own head and face with a knife, and demands the child,
64.13: but she sees it not till the re-establishment of the world [i.e. frashegird, cp. ch. 87 .]; this punishment she must suffer.'

65.2: whose chests were plunged in mud and stench,
65.3: and a sharp sickle ever went among their legs and other limbs;
65.4: and they ever called for a father and mother.
65.5: And I asked thus: 'Who are these souls?
65.6: and what sin was committed by them, whose souls suffer so severe a punishment?'
65.7: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
65.8: thus: 'These are the souls of that wicked who, in the world, distressed their father and mother;
65.9: and asked no absolution and forgiveness from their father and mother, in the world.'

66.1: I also saw the souls of a man and a woman
66.2: whose tongues were put out, and ever gnawed by the jaws of serpents.
66.3: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by the body of these?
66.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
66.6: thus: 'These are the souls of that wicked who, in the world, ever committed slander, and embroiled people together.'

67.1: I also saw the soul of a man
67.2: who was suspended by one leg in the darkness of hell [or hell of darkness];
67.3: and he had an iron sickle in his hand, and ever gashed his own chest and armpits [or loins],
67.4: and an iron spike was driven into his eye.
67.5: And I asked thus: 'Whose soul is this? and what sin was committed by him?'
67.6: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
67.7: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked man, to whom a city was confided for administration;
67.8: and that which was proper to do and order, was not done and not ordered;
67.9: and deficient weights and measures of capacity and length were kept,
67.10: and he listened to no complaints from the poor and from travellers [ lit. caravan people. see also ch. 68 and ch. 93 .].'

68.1: I also saw the souls of a man and a woman
68.2: whom they ever drag, the man to heaven and the woman to hell.
68.3: And the woman's hand was caught in the knot and sacred thread [kusti] of the man,
68.4: and she said thus: 'How is it when we had every benefit in union, among the living,
68.5: now they are dragging thee to heaven, and me to hell?'
68.6: And the man said thus: 'Because whatever things I received of the good and worthy and the poor, I also gave them back [meaning uncertain];
68.7: and I practised good thoughts and good words and good deeds;
68.8: I also heeded God, ad disregarded the demons;
68.9: and I have been steadfast in the good religion of the Mazdayasnians.
68.10: But you despised the good and poor and worthy and travellers;
68.11: you also disregarded God, and you worshipped idols;
68.12: and practised evil thoughts and evil words and evil deeds;
68.13: and you have been steadfast in the religion of Ahriman and the demons.'
68.14: And the woman said to the man
68.15: thus: 'Among the living, you yourself were completely lord and sovereign over me;
68.16: and my body and life and soul were yours;
68.17: and the food and income and clothing which I had, were from you;
68.18: then wherefore did you not chastise and punish me for it?
68.19: You have not even taught me, the reason of your goodness and excellence,
68.20: whereby you might have caused goodness and excellence in me,
68.21: and so now it would not be necessary to suffer this evil.'
68.22: And afterwards, the man went to heaven and the woman to hell.
68.23: And owing to the repentance of that woman, she was in no other affliction, in hell, but darkness and stench.
68.24: And that man sat in the midst of the pious of heaven, in shame from not converting and not teaching the woman, who might have become virtuous in his keeping.

69.1: I also saw the souls of women,
69.2: into both whose eyes a wooden peg was driven,
69.3: tied by one leg, head downwards.
69.4: And many frogs, scorpions, snakes, ants, flies, worms and other noxious creatures ( khrafstars ) went and came inside their jaws, noses, ears, posteriors and sexual parts.
69.5: And I asked thus: 'Whose souls are these?
69.6: and what sin was committed by them, whose souls suffer so severe a punishment?'
69.7: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
69.8: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked women who had a husband in the world,
69.9: and slept and granted cohabitation [i.e. sex] with another man;
69.10: and the bed of the husband was kept defiled, and his body injured.'

70.1: I also saw the souls of women whom they threw head downwards;
70.2: and something like a hedgehog, which had iron spikes grown from it, was introduced into the body and dropped back;
70.3: and from it, a finger dropping the semen of the demons and demonesses, which is stench and corruption, ever went into the inside of the jaws and nose.
70.4: And I asked thus: 'Who are those souls, who suffer such a punishment?'
70.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
70.6: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked women who, in the world, broke promises to their husbands,
70.7: and they have stayed away from the husband, and been never contented, and granted no cohabitation [i.e. sex].'

71.1:
*Sodomy and enticing wives to adultery.*
I also saw the soul of a man
71.2: whom the fangs of serpents stung and ever gnawed;
71.3: and in both eyes, snakes and worms ever voided;
71.4: and an iron spike was grown [scraped?] upon the tongue.
71.5: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this body, whose soul suffers so severe a punishment?'
71.6: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
71.7: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked man, by whom sodomy was much committed;
71.8: and through a desire for improper lust, he debauched the wives of others.
71.9: And his smooth speaking deceived and seduced the wives of others, and separated them from their husbands.'

72.1:
*Violating menstruation taboo*
I also saw the souls of women, by whom their own menstrual discharge was ever devoured.
72.2: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by the body of these, whose souls suffer so severe a punishment?'
72.3: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
72.4: thus: 'These are the souls of those women who heeded not their menstruation,
72.5: and injured water and fire and the earth of Spandarmad and Hordad and Amurdad,
72.6: and looked upon the sky and the sun and the moon,
72.7: and injured cattle and sheep with their menstruation,
72.8: and kept the pious man polluted.'

73.1:
*Makeup*
I also saw the souls of women
73.2: who ever shed and sucked and ate the blood and filth of their ten fingers;
73.3: and worms ever came into both eyes.
73.4: And I asked thus: 'Who are these souls?
73.5: and what sin was committed by them who suffer so severe a punishment?'
73.6: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
73.7: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked women who beautified their faces [with makeup], and kept the hair of others as ornament;
73.8: and they captivated the eyes of the men of God.'

74.1:
*Unlawfully slaughtering livestock.*
I also saw the souls of those who remained tied, head downwards, by one leg;
74.2: and a knife was driven into their hearts.
74.3: And I asked thus: 'Who are these souls?'
74.4: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
74.5: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked, by whom, in the world, beasts, cattle and sheep were unlawfully slaughtered and killed.'

75.1:
*Cruelty to animals.*
I also saw souls who were thrown under the feet of cattle,
75.2: struck by the horns, and their bellies torn, and bones broken; and they were groaning.
75.3: And I asked thus: 'Who are these people?'
75.4: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
75.5: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked, by whom, in the world, the mouths of beasts and ploughing cattle were muzzled;
75.6: and water was not given to them in the heat; and they were kept at work hungry and thirsty.'

76.1:
*Violating menstruation taboo and sorcery.*
I also saw the souls of women who ever lacerated their own breasts with their own hands and teeth;
76.2: and dogs ever tore and ate their bellies;
76.3: and both feet stood on hot brass.
76.4: And I asked thus: 'Whose souls are these? and what sin was committed by them?'
76.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
76.6: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked women who, in the world, prepared food during menstruation,
76.7: and brought it before a pious man, and bade him eat.
76.8: They also ever resorted to sorcery;
76.9: and they injured the earth of Spandarmad and the pious man.'

77.1:
*Cruelty to animals*
Then I saw souls whose backs, hands, and legs had wounds,
77.2: and they were suspended with the posteriors to the face [This sentence can also be read: 'head downwards in melted brass'; but the form avîtakht for 'melted' is unusual.];
77.3: and heavy stones ever rained in their backs.
77.4: And I asked thus: 'Who are those? and what sin was committed by them?'
77.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
77.6: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked who had beasts in the world,
77.7: and appointed them hard work, and made the burden unlawfully heavy,
77.8: and gave no sufficiency of food, so they suffered through leanness;
77.9: and when sores ensued, they were not kept back from work, and no remedy was provided.
77.10: Now they ( the souls ) must suffer such severe punishment.'

78.1:
*Adultery and infanticide*
Then I saw the soul of a woman
78.2: who ever dug an iron hill with her breasts;
78.3: and an infant cried from that side of the hill, and the cry ever continued;
78.4: but the infant comes not to the mother, nor the mother to the infant.
78.5: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this body, whose soul suffers so severe a punishment?'
78.6: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
78.7: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked woman who, in the world, became pregnant, not from her own husband, but from another person;
78.8: and she said thus: "I have bot been pregnant."

79.1:
*Corrupt judge.*
Then I saw the soul of a man,
79.2: both whose eyes were scooped out, and his tongue cut away;
79.3: and he remained suspended, in hell, by one leg;
79.4: his body also was ever raked with the two brazen prongs of a fork;
79.5: and an iron spike was driven into his head [or heart].
79.6: And I asked thus: 'What man is this? and what sin was committed by him?'
79.7: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
79.8: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked man whose justice, in the world, was false;
79.9: and he took bribes, and made false decisions.'

80.1:
*Falsifying measurements.*
Then I saw the souls of several who remained suspended, head downwards, in hell;
80.2: and they force the blood, filth, and brains of men into their mouths, and convey excrement into their noses;
80.3: and they [the tormentors?] ever cry thus: 'We keep just measures.'
80.4: And I asked thus: 'Who are these bodies? and what sin was committed by them?'
80.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
80.6: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked, by whom, in the world, weights and bushels and other small measures were kept short,
80.7: and things were sold to men.'

81.1:
*Adultery and sorcery*
Then I saw the soul of a woman whose tongue was cut away, and eyes scooped out;
81.2: and snakes, scorpions, worms, and other noxious creatures ( khrafstars ) ever devoured the brain of her head;
81.3: and from time to time, she seized her own body with the teeth, and ever gnawed the flesh.
81.4: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this body?'
81.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
81.6: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked woman who was, in her lifetime, an adultress.
81.7: she also practised much sorcery; and much mischief emanated from her.

82.1:
*Sharp tongue*
Then I saw the soul of a certain woman whose tongue was plucked out [Doubtful; it may mean 'whose tongues were many.'].
82.2: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this woman?'
82.3: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
82.4: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked woman whose tongue, in the world, was sharp;
82.5: and her husband and master was much troubled by her tongue.'

83.1: Then I saw the soul of a woman who ever ate her own dead refuse [nasa].
83.2: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this woman?'
83.3: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
83.4: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked woman who, in the world, ate much meat concealed from her husband,
83.5: and gave it to another person.'

84.1:
*Manufacturing and distributing narcotics*
Then I saw the soul of a woman
84.2: whose breasts they cut off; and her belly was torn, and the entrails given to the dogs.
84.3: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this woman?'
84.4: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
84.5: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked woman, by whom, in the world, poison and oil [liquor? infusion?] of opium were made and kept,
84.6: and given by her to people to eat.

85.1:
*Adultery*
Then I saw the soul of a woman,
85.2: on whose body they construct an iron coating,
85.3: and they turn back the mouth, and put it back to a hot oven.
85.4: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this woman?'
85.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
85.6: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked woman who was, among the living, the wife of a well-disposed and intelligent man;
85.7: and she broke her faith to her husband, and slept with a sinful and ill-disposed man.'

86.1:
*Khwetodas*
Then I saw the soul of a woman,
86.2: through whose body a grievous [prickly?] snake ascended, and came forth by the mouth.
86.3: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this body, where the soul suffers so severe a punishment?'
86.4: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
86.5: thus: ['This is the soul of that wicked woman who violated a next-of-kin [khwetodas] marriage.'

87.1:
*Infant neglect*
Then I saw the soul of a woman
87.2: who ever scraped her own body and face with an iron comb,
87.3: and ever dug an iron hill with her breasts.
87.4: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this woman?'
87.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
87.6: thus:] 'This is the soul of that wicked woman who, in the world, committed a crime,
87.7: and through a desire for wealth, gave no milk to her own infant.
87.8: And now she ever makes an outcry thus: "Here let me dig into this hill, that I may give milk to that infant."
87.9: Yet until the reestablishment of the world [Frashegird], she does not reach the infant.'

88.1:
*Improper sex and enticing wives to adultery*
Then I saw the soul of a man
88.2: who remained suspended, head downward, from a gibbet, and ever had sexual intercourse;
88.3: and they dropped semen into his mouth and ears and nose.
88.4: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this body, whose soul suffers so severe a punishment?'
88.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
88.6: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked man who, in the world, committed improper sexual intercourse;
88.7: and deceived and seduced the wives of others.'

89.1:
*Uncharitable*
Then I saw the souls of those who, on account of weakness, were dashed about from side to side in hell;
89.2: and they ever kept crying on account of thirst and hunger, cold and heat;
89.3: and noxious creatures ( khrafstars ) ever bit out of the back of their legs and other limbs.
89.4: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by those of these souls, who suffer so severe a punishment?'
89.5: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
89.6: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked whose food and clothing, in the world, were consumed by themselves,
89.7: and not given by them to the good and worthy; and they exercised no liberality whatever;
89.8: and they kept themselves, and the people who had come and remained under their control, hungry and thirsty and without clothing;
89.9: so they suffer cold and heat, hunger and thirst.
89.10: Now they are dead, and their wealth has remained for others;
89.11: now the soul suffers so severe a punishment from their own actions.'

90.1:
*Lying and profanity*
Then I saw the souls of those whom serpents sting and ever devour their tongues.
90.2: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by those, whose soul suffers so severe a punishment?'
90.3: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
90.4: thus: 'These are the souls of those liars and irreverent [or 'untruthful'] speakers who, in the world, spoke much falsehood and lies and profanity.'

91.1:
*Unfair judge*
Then I saw the soul of a man who slew his own child and ever ate the brains.
91.2: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this body, whose soul suffers so severe a punishment?'
91.3: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
91.4: thus: 'This is the soul of that sentencing judge who made unjust decisions between applicants for justice;
91.5: and plaintiffs and defendants were not looked upon, by him, favorably and justly;
91.6: but through a desire of wealth and covetousness, he shouted at suitors with anger and severity.'

92.1:
*Kept back benefits.*
Then I saw the souls of those, into whose eye a wooden peg was driven.
92.2: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by the body of these, whose soul suffers so severe a punishment?'
92.3: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
92.4: thus: 'These are the souls of those malicious ones who kept back benefits from mankind.'

93.1:
*Turning away travellers or charging for services*
Then I saw the souls of those who were fallen, headlong, into hell;
93.2: and smoke and heat were driven upon them from below, and a cold wind from above.
93.3: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by these bodies, whose souls suffer so severe a punishment?'
93.4: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
93.5: thus: 'These are the souls of those who, in the world, gave no place, nor caravanserai for travellers, nor lodging, nor space, nor baking oven;
93.6: or who gave them, and took hire for them.'

94.1:
*Starving their infants and selling the milk*
Then I saw the souls of those whose own breasts were placed upon a hot frying-pan, by their own hands,
94.2: and were ever turned from side to side.
94.3: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by these women, whose souls suffer so severe a punishment?'
94.4: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
94.5: thus: 'These are the souls of those women who gave their infants no milk, but emaciated and destroyed them;
94.6: and for worldly gain, gave milk to the infants of others.

95.1:
*Starved her infant, adultery*
Then I saw the soul of a woman who ever dug a hill with her breasts;
95.2: and was ever thirsty and hungry.
95.3: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this woman?'
95.4: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
95.5: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked woman who gave her infant no milk,
95.6: but left it hungry and thirsty;
95.7: and herself went with a strange man through a liking for avarice, and a lust for illicit intercourse.'

96.1:
*Didn't sow seed*
Then I saw the soul of a man whose tongue was cut out;
96.2: and they ever drag him by the hair, and scatter about the dead refuse [probably the hair pulled out by the roots], and measure it with a bushel.
96.3: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by this man, whose soul suffers so severe a punishment?'
96.4: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
96.5: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked man who, in the world, took seed,
96.6: and said thus: 'I will sow it;' and he sowed it not,
96.7: but ate it; and the earth of Spandarmad was defrauded.'

97.1:
*Falsehood*
Then I saw the souls of a man and a woman whose tongues were cut out.
97.2: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by these bodies, whose souls suffer so severe a punishment?'
97.3: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
97.4: thus: 'This is the soul of that wicked man and woman who, amongst the living, spoke much falsehood and profanity [or untruth],

98.1:
*Ate nasa, and killed an otter and other sacred animals*
Then I saw the souls of a woman and a man who voided and are up the excrement .
98.2: And I asked thus: 'What sin was committed by these bodies, whose souls suffer so severe a punishment?'
98.3: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
98.4: thus: 'These are the souls of that wicked man and woman who, in the world, devoured dead refuse through sinfulness;
98.5: and killed the water-otter in the water,
98.6: and smote and slew other creatures of Ohrmazd.'

99.1:
*Disobedient to rulers, enemies of their military*
Then I saw many more souls of wicked man and woman;
99.2: and they ever suffer terrible, fearful, hurtful, harmful, painful, dark, hellish torment and punishment of various kinds.
99.3: Then I saw souls whose tongues were scraped with a wooden peg;
99.4: and they ever went down, into hell, head foremost;
99.5: and the demons ever ploughed their whose bodies with an iron comb.
99.6: And I asked thus: 'Whose souls are these?
99.7: and what sin was committed by them whose souls suffer so severe a punishment?'
99.8: Srosh the pious, and Adar the angel, said
99.9: thus: 'These are the souls of those wicked who have been disobedient unto their rulers in the world,
99.10: and have been enemies of the armies and troops of their rulers.
99.11: Now they must here suffer such severe pain and torment and punishment.'

100.1:
*Ahriman (the devil)*
Then I saw the Evil spirit, the deadly, the world-destroyer, whose religion is evil,
100.2: who ever ridiculed and mocked the wicked in hell, and said
100.3: thus: 'Why did you ever eat the bread of Ohrmazd, and do my work?
100.4: and thought not of your own creator, but practiced my will?'
100.5: So he ever shouted to the wicked very mockingly.

101.1: Afterwards, Srosh the pious and Adar the angel took hold of my hand,
101.2: and brought me forth from that dark, terrible, fearful place,
101.3: and carried me to the eternal light, and the assembly of Ohrmazd and the archangels.
101.4: When I wished to offer homage before Ohrmazd.
101.5: And he was gracious and said thus: 'A perfect servant art thou, pious Arda Viraf, the messenger of the Mazdayasnians; go to the material world,
101.6: and as thou hast seen and understood, speak truly to the worlds;
101.7: for I, who am Ohrmazd, am with thee;
101.8: everyone who speaks correct and true, I honor and know;
101.10: And when Ohrmazd spoke in this manner, I remained astonished,
101.11: for I saw a light, but I saw nobody; I also heard a voice,
101.12: and I understood that: 'This is Ohrmazd'.
101.13: And he, the creator Ohrmazd, the most munificent of spirits, said
101.14: thus: 'Speak thou forth, Arda Viraf, to the Mazdayasnians of the world,
101.15: thus: 'There is only one way of piety, the way of the primitive religion, and the other ways are all no ways.
101.16: Take ye that one way which is piety, and turn ye not from it in prosperity, nor in adversity, nor in any way;
101.17: and practice good thoughts and good words and good deeds;
101.18: and remain in that same religion which, as received by him from me, Spitaman Zartosht and Vishtasp made current in the world;
101.19: and hold the proper law, but abstain from the improper.
101.20: And be ye aware also of this, that cattle are dust, and the horse is dust, and gold and silver are dust, and the body of man is dust;
101.21: he alone mingles not with the dust, who, in the world, praises piety and performs duties and good works.'
101.22: Perfect art thou, Arda Viraf! go and prosper;
101.23: since every purity and purification which you perform and keep,
101.24: and everything which you keep lawfully,
101.25: and the purification and ceremonial, when you perform them, in like manner, mindful of God, I know them all.'
101.26: And when I heard those words, I made a profound bow to the creator Ohrmazd.
101.27: And then, Srosh the pious, conveyed me successfully and courageously to this carpeted place.
101.28: May the glory of the good religion of the Mazdayasnians be triumphant!
101.29: Completed in health and pleasure and joy.

0.1: In the name of Hôrmazd, the lord, the greatest and wise, the all-ruling, all knowing, and almighty.
0.2: This is a book (kitâb), about the proper and improper, which is extracted from the good and pure religion of the Mazda-worshippers.
0.3: What is expedient (vâgib) is this, for every one to know and keep this in practice.
0.4: And it is not desirable that he become independent (‘hâlî) of this for a single hour (sâ’hat).
0.5: Because, when one becomes independent, the sin for each one may become abundant; and when it is brought into practice the reward becomes abundant.
0.6:
On this occasion (vaqt) I, a servant of the religion—like the môbad Erân-shâh, son (bin) of
Yazad-yâr, son of Tîstar-yâr, son of Âdar-bâd, son of Mâraspend —have sent a reward to their souls, unto every one who reads and is bound by duty.
0.7: Thus much (în qadar), which has come written, is a good work they know, whosoever are superior; but it is not possible for every one inferior to know of this.
0.8: If it were more (ziyâdat) it is proper, but if (imṃâ) less than this it is not proper to know; while, in gratitude for the benefits (sukr-i ni’hmat) of the sacred being, they become increasing in action, and the sacred being, the most high (ta’hâlâi), makes benefits occur on the spot on that account.
0.9: And, secondly, the kindness (lutf) and generosity (karm) of the sacred being, the most high, are manifest from this, that he created us with each member (âlat) complete (tamâm), and did not keep anything from the maternal nature.
0.10: And whatever was necessary for use he gave us.
0.11: At the head, likewise, he appointed a master, which is the wisdom for the purpose that they may keep these members in action.
0.12: May the peace of the sacred being, the most high, be on the souls of those acquainted with the religion of the pure Zaratust, the Spitamân, and of those who are pure and virtuous.
0.13: For the souls of those persons it is desirable that every duty they perform they shall perform through the authority (dastûrî) of the wisdom of the high-priests.

1.1: The first subject is this, that it is necessary that they become steadfast in the religion, and do not introduce any hesitation (sakk) and doubt into the heart.
1.2: And that they make a statement (‘haqîqat) with confidence (i’htiqâd), that the good religion, the true and perfect, which the Lord sent into the world (‘halq), is that which Zaratust has brought; which is this I hold.
1.3: Every time that mankind are like this, and do not introduce any hesitation and doubt into the heart, of every duty and good work that others have done, from the days of Zaratust until these days, and of whatever one does after this until the resurrection, there is a share for that person.
1.4: When the soul, on the fourth night, arrives at the head of the Kinvad bridge, the angel Mihir and the angel Rashn make up its account (‘hisâb) and reckoning.
1.5: And, if the good works it has done be deficient in quantity, of every duty and good work that those of the good religion have done in the earth of seven regions they appoint it a like portion (naʓîb), till the good works become more in weight; and the soul arrives righteous in the radiant locality of heaven.
1.6: For it is declared in revelation, that of the duty and good work which they perform in doubt—that is (ya’hnî), they entertain a suspicion like this, that 'I do not know that this faith, which I possess, is better in comparison with other faiths'—no merit whatever comes to their souls.
1.7: Therefore, the first (avval) thing is to become steadfast in the religion; and this is the chief of all good works.

2.1: The second subject is this, that it is necessary to make an effort (gahd), so that they may not commit any sin.
2.2: If even a trifling sin occurs it is not desirable to assume that this small quantity does not possess harm hereafter.
2.3: For it is said in revelation, that if such be the quantity of sin that the sin is one filament of the hair of the eyelashes more in weight than the good works are, that person arrives in hell.
2.4: And if such a quantity of good works be in excess, he arrives righteous in the radiant locality of heaven.
2.5: Therefore, even if a sin be trifling it is not desirable to commit it; and it is requisite to refrain, so that they may not commit it, and may become without doubt as to the religion.

3.1: The third subject is this, that it is necessary for man that he be continuously employed (masghûl) on his own work, and then the work becomes his own.
3.2: For it is declared in revelation, that every one who hereafter becomes employed on his own work, if in the midst of that work any trouble and discomfort happen to him, obtains in that other world twelve recompenses for every single instance.
3.3: If he becomes employed on iniquity (fasâd), and in the midst of that work any trouble and harm happen to him, he so obtains in that other world only torment (’huqûbat) and punishment.
3.4: Similarly (maTHalâm), if any one be himself going, employed on his own work, and a robber falls upon him on the road, and carries off his property (qumâs), or he be slain, they give him back in that other world four things for each one of whatever they have carried off.
3.5: If he be slain he becomes righteous, any sin that he has committed goes clean away from him, and they convey him to heaven.
3.6: But (ammâ) if he becomes faulty (bâtil) in any duty, and a robber falls upon him on the road, and carries off his wealth (mâl), or he be slain, when he descends to that other world all the property that other carried off from him becomes just as though it were his who has carried it off from that person; and, besides, there occur, as a substitute (’hivaʓ̣) for that property, the punishment and torment they give him.
3.7: And if he be slain it is just as though he who has carried it off from that person were one who had innocently slain that person who arrives in hell as retribution (mukâfât) for sin.

4.1: The fourth subject is this, that it is not desirable for any one that he should become hopeless of the pity (ra‘hmat) and forgiveness of Hôrmazd, and fix his heart outwardly on this, that our sin is excessive and it is not possible to arrive in heaven.
4.2: Because it happens that a small quantity of duty and good work is performed, and it may be that for that quantity Hôrmazd, the good and propitious, may have pity on him and may make him arrive in heaven.
4.3: For it is declared in revelation, that one time when Zaratust was in conversation with the sacred being, the most high, he saw a man whose whole body was in hell, and one foot—the right one —was outside of hell.
4.4: Zaratust enquired of the sacred being, the most high, thus: 'What person has this man been?'
4.5: Hôrmazd, the good and propitious, gave a reply (gavâb) thus: 'He has been a king, and possessed the sovereignty of thirty-three towns, and was conducting that sovereignty many years.
4.6: And he never did any virtuous action, but was committing much oppression, lawlessness, and violence (thulṁ).
4.7: By chance (qaʓ̣ârâ) he was one day going on the chase, and arrived out at a place (maûʓ̣a’h) and saw a goat that was tied.
4.8: A morsel of hay was placed very far off, and that goat was hungry.
4.9: Owing to this the goat was trying to eat the hay, but did not reach the hay.
4.10: This the king saw, and kicked his foot at that hay and cast it in front of the goat.
4.11: Now, in recompense for that, that one foot of his is outside of hell, and the remaining (bâqî) limbs are in hell.'
4.12: Therefore, although a sin has happened to any one, it is not necessary for him to become hopeless.
4.13: And whoever has the power (tâqat) is to endeavour to perform good works, so that there may be an atonement for the sin thereby; because the sacred being, the good and propitious, is kind to every one.

5.1: The fifth subject is this, that it is necessary for all those of the good religion that they make a thorough effort, so that they celebrate the ritual and become Navazûd.
5.2: For in our religion there is no good work more ample than this.
5.3: And it is declared in revelation, that, although much duty and good work be performed, it s not possible to attain to the supreme heaven (garôdmân), except on that one occasion when the Navazûd ceremony is performed, or they have celebrated a Gêtî-kharîd.
5.4: And on any occasion (‘hâl), if they are not able to perform it with their own hands, it is requisite to order it; and then it is inevitably necessary that the celebration of the Gêtî-kharîd should be in the same manner as they would have performed it with their own hands.
5.5: Man and woman are both equal in this good work; therefore, it is not proper to neglect this duty, for it is the chief of all the good works of the religion.
5.6: Because it is declared in revelation, that on the day that they are performing the Navazûd ceremony, or are celebrating a Gêtî-kharîd on his account, three times the soul of that person arrives at heaven, and they show it a place therein, and offer it a profuse greeting (niTHâr).
5.7: The explanation (tafsîr) of the Gâhs is this, that a Gâh—that is, that his own place—becomes visible to him in heaven that day.
5.8: And if one does not perform a Navazûd ceremony, or does not order the celebration of a Gêtî-kharîd, it is the same as when a poor (gharîb) man makes for a town, and does not obtain a spot where he may alight in that place.
5.9: Although it is his own town he is in this trouble.
5.10: Therefore, it is not possible to bring to hand a place in heaven through any good work, except by the performance of the Navazûd ceremony, or by ordering the celebration of a Gêtî-kharîd.
5.11: And a Gêtî-kharîd is this, that heaven is purchased in the world, and one's own place brought to hand in heaven.

6.1: The sixth subject is this, that of the many good works there are those which, when they accomplish them, obtain great (’hathîm) rewards; and if one does not perform them severe punishment seizes upon one at the head of the Kinvad bridge.
6.2: One is the celebration of the season festivals; the second is keeping the days of the guardian spirits; the third is attending to the souls of fathers, mothers, and other relations; the fourth is reciting the Khûrshêd Nyâyis three times every day; the fifth is reciting the Mâh Nyâyis three times every month, once when it becomes new, once when it becomes full, and once when it becomes slender; and the sixth is celebrating the Rapithwin ceremony once every year.
6.3: If not able to celebrate them oneself, it is requisite to order them, so that they may celebrate them every single time.
6.4: These six good works are things indispensable unto every one.
6.5: When any one of them is not performed—be it that which, if omitted at its own time, it is not possible to accomplish, or if it be that one time one omits an occasion, and another time they accomplish twice as much—one should consider that as an advantage, which occurs in retribution for it, or as atonement for the transgression.
6.6: Because they call the transgression of each of these six a bridge-sin; that is, every one through whom a transgression of these may have arisen they keep back, at the head of the Kinvad bridge, till punishment for it happens to him, and no good work is possible in this place, which is torment and punishment for him.
6.7: Therefore it is necessary to make an effort, that they may be performed each one at its own time, so that they may obtain a recompense, and not a severe punishment.

7.1: The seventh subject is this, that, when a sneeze (’hatsat) comes forth from any one, it is requisite to recite one Yathâ-ahû-vairyô and one Ashem-vohû.
7.2: Because there is a fiend in our bodies, and she is an adversary who is connected with mankind, and strives so that she may make misfortune (’hillat) and sickness predominant (mustaûlî) over mankind.
7.3: And in our bodies there is a fire which they call a disposition—in Arabic they say tabî’hat—and they call it the sneezing instinct (gharîzî).
7.4: It is connected with that fiend, and they wage warfare, and it keeps her away from the body of man.
7.5: Then, as the fire becomes successful over that fiend, and puts her to flight (hazîmat), a sneeze comes because that fiend comes out.
7.6: Afterwards, because it is necessary, they recite these inward prayers and perform the benediction (âfrîn) of the fire, so that it may remain for a long period while thou art keeping this fiend defeated.
7.7: When another person hears the sneeze, it is likewise requisite for him to utter the said prayers, and to accomplish the benediction of that spirit.

8.1: The eighth subject is this, that it is necessary to maintain the religion by rule (dastûr), and to practise obedience to the commands of the high-priests; and every duty that people perform they should perform by their authority.
8.2: For it is declared in the good religion, that, if they accomplish as many good works as the leaves of the trees, or the sand-grains of the desert, or the drops (qatrah) of rain, which they do not perform by command of the high-priests, or to their satisfaction, no merit whatever attains to their souls, and for the good works they have done they obtain sin as a recompense.
8.3: While such a one is living it is not proper to call him righteous, and when he dies he does not attain to heaven, and not a single archangel comes near him.
8.4: He does not make his escape from the hands of the demons and Aharman, and he does not obtain a release from hell.
8.5: Because duties and good works attain to the soul on those occasions when they perform them with the authority of the high-priests and those acquainted with the religion, and when they give them one-tenth of those good works.

9.1: The ninth subject is this, that it is necessary to practise abstinence from committing or permitting unnatural intercourse.
9.2: For this is the chief of all sins in the religion: there is no worse sin than this in the good religion, and it is proper to call those who commit it worthy of death in reality.
9.3: If any one comes forth to them, and shall see them in the act, and is working with an axe, it is requisite for him to cut off the heads or to rip up the bellies of both, and it is no sin for him.
9.4: But it is not proper to kill any person without the authority of high-priests and kings, except on account of committing or permitting unnatural intercourse.
9.5:
For it says in revelation that unnatural intercourse is on a par with Aharman, with Afrâsiyâb, with Dahâk, with Tûr-i Brâdar-vakhṣh who slew
Zaratust, with Malkôs who will arise, with the serpent Sruvar which existed in the days of Sâm Narîmân, and as many sins as are theirs.
9.6: And Aharman, the evil one, becomes more joyful, owing to this practice, than owing to the other sins which have made high-priests necessary; for the soul itself of that person becomes extinct.
9.7: And when they commit the sin with women, it is just the same as that with men.

10.2: Because the sacred thread-girdle is to be a girding of the loins and to preserve obedience (tâ’hat) to the Lord, may he be honoured and glorified (’hazza va galla)!
10.3: The first person who set the wearing of this sacred thread-girdle in view was Jamshêd.
10.4: And it may be the whole (gumlah) of the demons and fiends who are made extinct by the glory of wearing the sacred thread-girdle.
10.5:
Every one who has tied the sacred thread-girdle round the waist is out of the department of Aharman, and is established in the department of
Hôrmazd.
10.6: And also, while he keeps the sacred thread-girdle on the waist, there is a share for him of all those duties and good works which they perform in the earth of seven regions.
10.7: It is like that which occurs when they are performing hamâ zôr and hamâ ashô, and have put on this sacred thread-girdle on that account, or when, similarly, some one in Kasmîr, or Erân-veg, or Kangdez, or the enclosure formed by Jam, performs a good work, and we are not able to perform it with hamâ zôr, then they and we, who wear the sacred thread-girdle on the waist, are mutually connected and equally meritorious, one with the other.
10.8: As no good work attains to him who does not wear a sacred thread-girdle—excepting that which he performs himself—it is therefore necessary that any one of mankind should not put it away from the waist on any occasion, so that the associated good works of those of the good religion may attain to him.
10.9: And those four knots, with which they tie it on, are on this account, that it may give four attestations.
10.10: The first knot is that which preserves constancy (qarâr), and gives attestation as to the existence, unity, purity, and matchlessness of the sacred being, the good and propitious.
10.11: The second knot is that which gives attestation that it is the good religion of the Mazda-worshippers which is the word of the sacred being.
10.12: The third knot is that which gives attestation as to the apostleship and mission (rasûlî) in the just (‘haqq) Zaratust, the Spitamân.
10.13: The fourth knot is that which adduces more pleasantly, gives assurance (iqrâr), and openly accepts that I should think of good, speak of good, and do good.
10.14: And from the whole I become established; and the pure, good religion is this, that I persist in those views.
10.15: And, again, when the archangels came meeting Zaratust they likewise wore the sacred thread-girdle on the waist; and the distinctive characteristic (farq) amid the laws of the sacred being is the wearing of the sacred thread-girdle.
10.16: It is incumbent both on woman and on man, and it is altogether (albattah) improper when they do not wear it.

11.1: The eleventh subject is this, that it is necessary to maintain the fire-place properly, and to keep watch, so that the fire shall not die out, and that nothing polluted and impure shall attain to the fire; and it is necessary to make a menstruous woman avoid being within three steps of it.
11.2: Because every time that they maintain a fire properly, which is within a dwelling, every fire which is in the earth of seven regions becomes pleased with those persons, and, when they ask a favour, or beg a necessity (‘hâgat), it becomes quickly operative.
11.3: And every time that one does not maintain it properly, every fire which is in the earth of seven regions receives injury from that person, and the necessity he begs does not become operative.
11.4: If any one does not maintain the fire-place properly, if he gives a hundred dînârs to the fire Gusasp there is no acceptance of it, and that sin does not depart from him.
11.5: For it is declared in revelation, that the creator Hôrmazd has given sovereignty in heaven to Ardibahist, the archangel, and has spoken thus: 'As to every one with whom thou art not pleased, do not let him escape into heaven.'
11.6: And this is also declared in revelation, that, every time that they do not maintain the fire properly, pregnancy becomes scarcer for the women, fewer male children are born, and honour (‘hurmat) in the vicinity of the king becomes less for the men, and there is no approbation (qabûl) of their words.
11.7: For every single fire which dies out in a dwelling a loss of three dirhams and two dângs falls on the property of that person, or it becomes the loss of this dwelling, or it does not reach him from the place whence wealth comes to him.

12.1: The twelfth subject is this, that, when any one dies, an order is necessary that how much soever scantier clothing they are able to make a beginning of, the better they act.
12.2: Beside (illâ) something become old and washed, anything new is not proper for the purpose that they may let it go upon a dead body.
12.3: For in the commentary of the Vendîdâd it asserts that, if they shall pass on to a dead body as much as a woman's spindle makes for a single thread, with the exception of that which is unavoidable, for every single thread a black snake hangs, in that other world, on to the liver of that person who has made a beginning of the clothing.
12.4: Likewise, that dead person becomes his antagonist (‘haʓ̣m), and hangs similarly upon his skirt, and speaks thus: 'This clothing, which thou hast put on my body, devours me, having become worms and noxious creatures.
12.5: My name was put upon a sacred cake, the fourth day, with a Yast, so that there might be alike a benefit therefrom for my soul, and it might be alike unnecessary for thee to bear this torment (’haDHâb).'
12.6: Owing to that, many sorrows come to that person, and he has no advantage from it.
12.7: Therefore, it is necessary to act with caution (i’htiyât), so that, how much soever the clothing be scantier, they may make a beginning of it.
12.8: And as many as shall be able to walk after the bier (tâbût) and corpse shall walk.
12.9: Because every step that they go after a corpse is a good work of three hundred stîrs; and every stîr is four dirhams, in such manner that three hundred stîrs are a thousand and two hundred dirhams.
12.10: For every single step there is thus much good work.

13.1: The thirteenth subject is this, that it is necessary to maintain the souls of fathers, mothers, and relations properly.
13.2: And, when any day of theirs occurs, it is necessary to make an endeavour, so that they may accomplish the ceremonial (yazisn), the sacred feast (myazd), the consecration of the sacred cakes (drôn), and the benedictions (âfrîngân).
13.3: For it is declared in revelation, that, every time that any day of theirs occurs, they will bring with themselves 9999 guardian spirits of the righteous, like that case when any one goes home himself, and brings people (qaûm) in hospitality.
13.4: And, when they utter the consecration of the sacred cakes and sacred feast and the benedictions, those people become joyful and utter blessings on that house and master of the house, and on the house-mistress and any persons who are in that house.
13.5: But if they do not celebrate the sacred feast, the consecration of the sacred cakes, the ceremonial, and the benedictions, the spirits will remain for them in that place from dawn as long as the period of a day, and are maintaining a hope that 'perhaps they will have us in remembrance.'
13.6: Then, if they do not bring them into remembrance, the souls turn upwards from that place, go very quickly on high, and will say, 'O creator Hôrmazd! they do not know that we are such as we are, and that it is necessary for them to come into this world, and in this world they will not give any one acquittal.
13.7: For them there is need of the good works in consecrating the sacred cakes and celebrating the sacred feast and benedictions; there is no need of them for such as we.
13.8: Yet (va lîkin), if they would have maintained a place for the duty of those days, we should have turned away from them misfortunes of various kinds; but, as they have not maintained observance of us in the day's duty, we are not able to come in friendship to this house.'
13.9: Thus much they say, and turn away in anger, and go away from that place.

14.1: The fourteenth subject is this, that, when the nails are pared according to custom (ba-‘hilâl), it is necessary that they put the parings into a paper.
14.2: And it is further necessary to take the Srôsh-bâz inwardly, and to utter three Yathâ-ahû-vairyôs.
14.3: And for the speaking of this—to say with each Yathâ-ahû-vairyô —the Avesta is this:—Paiti tê, meregha Ashô-zusta! imau srvau vaêdhayêmi, imau srvau âwaêdhayêmi; imause tê srvau, meregha Ashô-zusta! hyâre arstayaska, karetayaska, thanvareka, ishavaska erezifyô-parena, asnaka fradakhshanya paiti daêvô-Mâzainyãn; ashâ vohû mananghâ yâ sruyê pare magaonô.
14.4: Afterwards, one completes the Bâz in the manner that it was taken inwardly.
14.5: At those two Yathâ-ahû-vairyôs, with which one completes the Bâz, at each one, he makes lines (‘hatthâ) in a little dust in the midst of the nail-parings.
14.6: And, if he does not know this Bâz, on uttering the Srôsh-bâz and those three Yathâ-ahûvairyôs he is to furrow three lines, with the nail-cutter, around the nail-parings, and then he is to complete the Bâz with those Yathâ-ahû-vairyôs, and to put the dust, with the end of the nail-cutter, into the midst of the nail-parings, and carry them to a desert spot.
14.7: It is necessary that he should carry a hole down through four finger-breadths of earth, and, having placed the nail-parings in that spot, he puts the soil overhead.
14.8: For Hôrmazd, the good and propitious, has created a bird which they call Ashô-zust, and they call it the bird of Bahman.
14.9: They also call it the owl, and it eats nails.
14.10: It is altogether necessary that they do not leave them unbroken, for they would come into use as weapons (silâ‘h) of wizards.
14.11: And they have also said that, if they fall in the midst of food, there is danger of pulmonary consumption.

15.1: The fifteenth subject is this, when one sees anything that is welcome to the eyes, it is requisite to say 'in the name of the sacred being.'
15.2: Because, if they do not say 'in the name of the sacred being,' and an injury happens to that thing, or a disaster occurs, one becomes a sinner; so far is notorious (ma’hlûm).

16.1: The sixteenth subject is this, that, when a woman becomes pregnant in a house, it is necessary to make an endeavour so that there may be a continual fire in that house, and to maintain a good watch over it.
16.2: And, when the child becomes separate from the mother, it is necessary to burn a lamp for three nights and days—if they burn a fire it would be better—so that the demons and fiends may not be able to do any damage and harm; because, when a child is born, it is exceedingly delicate for those three days.
16.3: For it is declared in revelation, that, when Zaratust, the Spitamân, became separate from his mother, every night, for three nights, a demon came on, with a hundred and fifty other demons, so that they might effect the slaughter (halâk) of Zaratust, and, when they had beheld the light of the fire, they had fled away, and had not been able to do any damage and harm.
16.4: During forty days it is not proper that they should leave the child alone; and it is also not proper that the mother of the infant should put her foot over a threshold in the dwelling, or cast her eyes upon a hill, for it is bad for her menstruation.

17.1: The seventeenth subject is this, that when they cut a toothpick (‘hilâl), or a splinter which they wish to apply to the root of the teeth, it is necessary that they retain no bark.
17.2: For if a small quantity of bark be on it when they apply it to the teeth, and they cast it away, if a pregnant woman puts her foot upon it, the danger of that may be that the child comes to harm.

18.1: The eighteenth subject is this, that it is necessary for mankind to make an endeavour, so that they may espouse a wife in their youth and beget a child.
18.2: And for women, in like manner, it is necessary that there should be a longing (raghbat) for espousing a husband.
18.3: Because it is declared in revelation, that every duty and good work a child performs becomes the father's and mother's, just like those which they have performed with their own hands.
18.4: The meaning (ma’hnî) of pûr ('a son') is that which signifies pûl ('a bridge'), for by this bridge they arrive at that other world.
18.5: If there be no child for any one they call him one with a severed bridge, that is, the way for him to that other world is severed, and he is not able to attain to that world.
18.6: At the head of the Kinvad bridge he shall remain; although he has performed much duty and good works he is not able to make a passage over the Kinvad bridge, and they do not make up his account and reckoning.
18.7: And every archangel that comes forward to that place first asks these words, that is, 'Hast thou brought thy own substitute visibly into the world, or not?'
18.8: When he has not brought it, they will pass over him, and his soul will remain, in that place, full of anguish and grief (gham).
18.9: A similitude (miTHâl) of it is like that which happens when any one may be in a wilderness, and there may be fear of wild animals and creatures, and near to him may be his own town, but a river of water is in front, and it is not possible to make a passage over that river, as a bridge is fallen in, and he is not able to arrive at that town, but he is always upon the bank (sart) speaking thus: 'Would that the bridge would become perfect!'
18.10: The duty as to children is in this aggregate.
18.11: Therefore, the creator Hôrmazd has granted unto men that, if there be any one to whom sickness from heaven may occur, and there be no provision of a child for him, he has commanded him that he should make some one a son of his own, as a friend of his soul, and should receive a child, because every duty can be delegated.
18.12: That person is in place of a child, and every duty and good work that he performs shall be just like that which is performed by one's own hand.
18.13: And, finally, if any one departs from the world (dunyâ) and possesses no adopted child, it is incumbent on the priests and high-priests and his relations to appoint his adopted son, and it is necessary to bring some one in sight on that account, so that his soul may spring away from the torment of hell.
18.14: Because, every time that his relations do not pay attention to this, when they proceed to that other world, the soul of that person hangs about them and speaks thus: 'I left with you something that I had collected and borne trouble for in many years, and you seized upon it, and put it into your own expenditure (‘harg), and did not seek for mercy (safqat) on my soul.
18.15: In the same manner as I have remained, delayed (maûqûf) in this place, I will not let you pass; so that you will make no passage over the Kinvad bridge till the sacred being takes my rights away from you.'
18.16: Then the angel Rashn and the angel Mihir make up their reckoning, and, as to whatever those persons have seized upon from the other's property, for every single dînâr the account makes four, and they take away the equivalent.
18.17: And, as in that world there are no gold and silver, they take away from their souls the good works that they have done, and they give them to the soul of this other.
18.18: Still, while others do not appoint the adopted son, they are not able to pass over the Kinvad bridge, nor to arrive at their own station.
18.19: There is no duty whatever more incumbent on relations than this duty, and every time that they appoint an adopted son for any one it is just as though they have made the deceased alive; and there are no limit (‘hadd) and end (nihâyat) of their good works.

19.1: The nineteenth subject is this, that the performance of agriculture is like that when some one is performing the ceremonial of the sacred beings, and it is necessary to maintain much respect for agriculturists; it is also necessary to keep trouble and strife far from them.
19.2: For it is declared in revelation, that, as to every one who replants a shrub, while that shrub or tree exists at the place, every good work that every one, who eats of that shrub, does in that state of repletion becomes the agriculturist's, just like those which are done by his own hand.
19.3: If any one orders it, just as that good work occurs much new repose (râ‘hat) and comfort reach his soul.
19.4: As to corn and grain (‘hubûb) and whatever they sow, it is just like this, because, as regards every one who eats wheat, barley, and other grains, and performs duty and good works, they become those of the sower of those grains, just as those which are performed by his own hand.
19.5: Because, for the life of mankind a crop was necessary, the creation of a creator after the sacred being, the most high, owing to the work of the agriculturist.
19.6: For every one who eats anything dies, therefore, as regards that person by whose work the life of mankind is established, it is necessary to consider him valuable and precious.

20.1: The twentieth subject is this, that it is incumbent on those of the good religion that they continually give something to the worthy to eat, on account (gihat) of that which it says in revelation thus: 'When thou givest things to some one that he may eat, every duty and good work that he performs in that state of repletion become those of that person, who has given that bread or food to him, just like those which he has performed with his own hand.'
20.2: And if he commits a sin, he who may have given food to him is innocent.
20.3: But it is necessary that he be of the good religion and worthy; they should give something to one of a different religion only in case of extreme necessity (ʓ̣arûrat), lest it become as a sin.

21.1: The twenty-first subject is this, that, when they eat bread, it is necessary that one should recite the Ithâ-âd-yazamaidê and three Ashem-vohûs, especially (ba-‘hâʓʓatam) in the benediction-ceremonies (âfrîngân).
21.2: For it is declared in the good religion of the Mazda-worshippers, that, when they wish to celebrate the sacred feast (myazd) and benediction-ceremonies, it is necessary that all persons who are seated at the feast should take up the inward prayer.
21.3: For each man an angel is stationed, on the right-hand side, and two angels for the priests.
21.4: But when they eat chatteringly, or relate the news (‘hadîTH), the angels depart from them, and a demon seizes on the place of each angel.
21.5: And in former times the custom (’hâdat) of the people would have been in this manner, that, if any one should have come to the door in the middle of the feast, that person whose Âfrîngân-precinct it might have been, or whoever should have gone to the expense of that Âfrîngân, would have had words with that intruding person, and would have also spoken thus: 'As thou hast brought my feast to harm, give me back whatever has been the cost.'
21.6: And in one place in revelation it is declared that from eating chatteringly itself is the sin, for every one who is chattering during the eating of bread is just like him who is smiting and harassing the angels of the spiritual existences.
21.7: Therefore, if there be any one who is not able to consecrate a sacred cake, it is necessary to eat bread with the inward prayer of Hôrmazd, that is, the archangels.
21.8: And, if he does not altogether know it, he recites the Ithâ-âd-yazamaidê and three Ashem-vohûs, and eats up the bread.
21.9: Afterwards he makes his mouth clean, and, four Ashem-vohûs and two Yathâ-ahû-vairyôs being spoken out, he is then to utter words.
21.10: For, every time that this custom (qâ’hidat) is carried on in a place, through the first Ashem-vohû so much good work has arisen that it has propitiated the sacred being, the good and propitious; through the second Ashem-vohû so much good work has arisen that it has reverenced and propitiated Srôsh, the righteous; through the third Ashem-vohû so much good work has arisen that it has reverenced and propitiated Khurdâd and Ameredâd, the archangels; and through the fourth Ashem-vohû so much good work has arisen that whatever the creator Hôrmazd has created becomes reverenced and propitiated.
21.11: And with each mouthful (luqmah) that is eaten, while the inward prayer subsists, they proclaim a blessing for Khurdâd and Ameredâd, the archangels.
21.12: But, if it be eaten without the inward prayer, as demons are in that place, they say, 'Thou mightest have eaten the poison of a serpent.'
21.13: Therefore, take notice as to which is the better of these two.

22.1: The twenty-second subject is this, that the performance of Gâdangôî ('intercession') is like that when some one is occasioning the ceremonial of the sacred beings.
22.2: Therefore, it should be expedient that it be continuous, and that they perform Gâdangôî as regards the priests and high-priests and the worthy.
22.3: For, in the commentary of the Hâdôkht Nask, it says that every one who performs Gâdangôî, and extracts anything from a person on their account, and conveys it to them, is as much without dishonesty (‘hiyânat), towards them, as he who may have given to them out of his own property.
22.4: And in the spiritual existence they take account of that profit for him, and just as they make out the account of the good work of that person who may have given it, even so much is his good work.

23.1: The twenty-third subject is this, that it is requisite to restrain a tethered animal from misbehaviour, and to keep watch over one's own creatures, especially at the time when they have eaten meat.
23.2: Therefore, if they have eaten meat and they commit an assault, every offence that the animal (‘haîvân) commits may be that person's whose meat may be eaten.
23.3: For example, if a horse lashes out a kick (lakad) at any one, the offence may be that person's whose food may be eaten and caused the offence.
23.4: Therefore it is necessary to make an endeavour that they shall commit no offence whatever, especially at a time when they have eaten meat.

24.1: The twenty-fourth subject is this, that when an infant is born from its mother it is necessary that they give it the consecrated Hôm-juice, on this account, that understanding (’haql), wisdom, and knowledge may more abundantly get to it, and the want (ablat) of them may come more scantily upon it.
24.2: If, at that time, they do not perform the consecration, they should take forth a little Hôm for it, and recite a Yathâ-ahû-vairyô, and put a trifle of water into it, and make Hôm-juice of that, and give it to the infant, and afterwards milk.

25.1: The twenty-fifth subject is this, that any agreement and promise (qaûl) they make with any one it is necessary so far to perform and bring to pass.
25.2: Although many things may go to harm by means (sabab) of it, it is not desirable to perform that agreement with duplicity.
25.3: Because, in our religion, they call this a Mihir-drug ('breach of promise'), and in revelation it decrees, as to any one who commits a Mihir-drug, that the way to heaven becomes closed for him, and that person himself goes discomforted out of this world, so that a warning (’halâmat) becomes quite manifest unto him.
25.4: And a Mihir-drug is attached in such a manner that, if fortune (tâli’h) may have befallen any one happily, or an insufficient quantity of his life (’humr) may have remained, the Mihir-drug extends to his children without opposition (‘hilâf).
25.5: And every household that becomes extinct, or race whose issue fails, or any of the great misfortunes that happen to mankind—from which misfortune one obtains release with difficulty—may all be owing to the fact that they have committed a Mihir-drug.
25.6: If committed by oneself, it is declared, in one place in revelation, that the glorified Zaratust, the Spitamân, enquired of Hôrmazd, the good and propitious, thus: 'Of any of the sins that mankind commit which is the worst?'
25.7: Hôrmazd, the good and propitious, decreed thus: 'No sin whatever is worse than this, that two persons make a covenant with one another in such a manner that no one whatever is between them, except me who am Hôrmazd; and, afterwards one of those two persons deviates from it, and says, "I have no knowledge (‘habar) of it," and no one whatever is a witness, for that other person, except me.'
25.8: No sin whatever is worse than that, and that person himself will not go out of this world until retribution overtakes him, and in that other world his punishment is more severe than all; so that person becomes unfortunate in both worlds.
25.9: And it is the same if this covenant be with a righteous person or a wicked one.

26.1: The twenty-sixth subject is this, that the wise and the ancients say that when a man becomes fifteen years of age it is necessary that he takes one of the angels as his own protection, that he takes one of the wise as his own sage, and that he takes one of the high-priests and officiating priests as his own high-priest.
26.2: So that, if, any time, a bereavement (âstânah) approaches, he may beg a favour from the archangels, in order that it may furnish an escape from that bereavement.
26.3: And, any time any affair comes forward, and he has to have opinion (râî) and advice (masvarat), he holds a consultation with that sage, while the sage tells him his opinion (tadbîr).
26.4: And, if any question as to proper and improper comes forward, he speaks with that high-priest, so that he may tell him in reply.
26.5: When the instructions of these three persons are brought to pass, carrying out the commands of the sacred being is accomplished.
26.6:
Especially the instructions of the high-priests, because their satisfaction is connected with the satisfaction of the sacred being; and the high-priests possess so much dignity (martabat) in the presence of the sacred being, the good and propitious, that they are quite able to forgive any trivial one of the sins of mankind, and Hôrmazd, the good and propitious, quickly forgives that sin for the high-priest. 7.
Therefore, carrying out the commands of the high-priests becomes incumbent on every one; and the fulfilment of this maxim is better than that of a whole assemblage of maxims.

27.1: The twenty-seventh subject is this, that is, if any affair comes forward, that they should thoroughly understand whether it be a good work, or a sin.
27.2: In that manner it becomes better that they make an evasion on the spot, until a time when they make it known with accuracy that that affair is a sin or a reward.
27.3: If they perform any affair without knowing this, although it be a good work, it becomes a sin for them.
27.4: For it is declared in revelation, that, except that which they enquire of the high-priests, no affair whatever is proper to perform.
27.5: Whatever wisdom there be for any one from his own head is only one; then, as two wisdoms are more than one, it therefore makes it expedient to enquire of the high-priests.

28.1: The twenty-eighth subject is this, that, when they teach the Avesta, it is in like manner necessary that they teach it properly and truly, and recite it with deliberation and composure (sâkinî).
28.2: And it is necessary for those who are taught to recite it connectedly, and to keep it ever in remembrance.
28.3: For it is declared in revelation, that the sacred being has decreed thus: 'As to every one who puts the Avesta away from his memory, I will put his soul as far from heaven as the width of the earth.'
28.4: And in the commentary of the Avesta it is related that, in former times, as to any one who had been taught the Avesta and had put it away from his memory, until the time he had again made it easy, they would have given him bread like that which they give to the dogs.
28.5: And in another place I have read that they would have given bread to him on the point of a spear.

29.1: The twenty-ninth subject is this, that, when they provide any munificence (sa‘hâvat) or liberality, it is necessary that they provide it for the worthy; and one is to consider thus: 'Is this person, to whom I am giving this thing, worthy or not?'
29.2: Therefore it is necessary to make an effort, so that they may not give to the unworthy.
29.3: For in revelation, as regards that person who provides any munificence for the unworthy, they call it a vain work and a gift without advantage; and day by day it is the punishment and torment of that person.
29.4: And, whatever they give to the unworthy, they have made that thing extinct.

30.1: The thirtieth subject is this, that it is not proper to pour away water at night, especially from the northern side (gânib) which would be the worst.
30.2: Therefore, if it become a necessity in the end (ba-‘hatam), it is requisite to recite one Yathâ-ahû-vairyô, and, when they make a light ready (‘hâʓ̣ir), to pour away the water gently.
30.3: In like manner it is not proper to swallow water at night, because it is a sin.
30.4: But, if a necessity arises, it is necessary to make a light ready, and one first eats some morsels of food (ta’hâm) so that the sin may be less.

31.1: The thirty-first subject is this, that, every time they eat bread, it is necessary to withhold three morsels from their own bodies, and to give them to a dog.
31.2: And it is not desirable to beat a dog.
31.3: For, of the poor no one whatever is poorer than a dog, and it is necessary to give a tethered animal bread, because the good work is great.
31.4: And in revelation it is declared in this manner, that, if a dog is asleep upon the road, it is not proper that they put a foot violently on the ground, so that he becomes awake.
31.5: And, in former times, an allowance (râtib) of bread would have been made every day for the sake of the dogs, three times in summer and twice in winter, on this account, that one wishes them to come to the assistance of his soul at the Kinvad bridge.
31.6: In the worldly existence they are the guard of men and cattle.
31.7: If there had not been a dog they would not have been able to keep a single sheep.
31.8: Every time that he barks, just as his bark goes forth, the demons and fiends run away from the place.

32.1: The thirty-second subject is this, that, when a hen utters a crow in a house, or the cock crows. unseasonably, it is desirable that they do not kill it, and do not consider it a bad habit (fa’hl).
32.2: Because it is uttering that crow for the reason that a fiend has found a way into that house, and the hen or the cock, alone, does not possess the power (tâqat) that would keep the fiend away from that house, and the hen is going to give the cock assistance, and utters the crow.
32.3: Therefore, if any time the chance (ittifâq) happens in that manner, it is requisite to bring another cock, so that they may drive away that fiend through the assistance of one another.
32.4: And if a cock crows unseasonably it is likewise not desirable to kill it, because the reason may be this which I have stated.
32.5: For it is declared in the good religion, that there is a fiend whom they call Sêg, and, in every house where an infant exists, that fiend strives that she may cause some misfortune to come upon that house.
32.6: So it is necessary that they should keep a cock on the watch for her, so that it may smite that fiend and force her to the road away from that house.

33.1: The thirty-third subject is this, that, when there is a place and any risk or fear exists that a corpse is concealed beneath the ground, one is to make it apparent and visible, because it is a great good work.
33.2: For it is declared in the good religion, that, when they conceal a corpse beneath the ground, Spendârmad, the archangel, shudders; it is just as severe as a serpent or scorpion would be to any one in private sleep, and is also just like that to the ground.
33.3: When thou makest a corpse beneath the ground as it were apparent, thou makest the ground liberated from that affliction.

34.1: The thirty-fourth subject is this, that it is greatly necessary to refrain from much slaughter of animals and the cattle species.
34.2: Because it says in revelation that, for every one who slaughters many animals and cattle, every fibre of the hair of a goat becomes, in that other world, like a sharp sword, and adheres in the soul of that person.
34.3: And there are several things the slaughter of which is very bad, and the sin very abundant, as the lamb, the kid, the ploughing ox, the war horse, the swallow bird that catches the locust, and the cock; and of the whole of these the sin is most as regards the cock.
34.4: If it becomes a necessity, it is proper to kill a cock that does not crow, and it is necessary to consecrate their heads.
34.5: Any head of an animal, not consecrated, it is not desirable to eat, so that it becomes so far a righteous gift.
34.6: If one be not able to consecrate the head, it is requisite to consecrate one kidney as a substitute (badal) for it.

35.1: The thirty-fifth subject is this, that, when they wish to wash the face, they should recite ore Ashem-vohû, and set the mouth firmly closed, so that the water, not staying away from it, shall not go into the mouth.
35.2: And, as one washes over the face, they should recite the Kem-nâ-mazdâ, so that the fiend Nasrust may become smitten.

36.1: The thirty-sixth subject is this, that it is strictly incumbent on mankind, on man and woman, to perform the Bareshnûm ceremony, because mankind feed on menstruous matter in the womb of the mother.
36.2: For that reason it is necessary to perform the Bareshnûm once, so that one may become pure from that pollution.
36.3: For if one becomes fifteen years of age, and does not perform the Bareshnûm, whatever he puts a hand on, the glory and purity of that thing will diminish; and it is not proper that they put a hand on a sacred cake or any thing washed with ceremony.
36.4: In revelation it says, if any one who has not performed the Bareshnûm shall die, the demons make him as though he were a corpse kept one month in the hot season.
36.5: And, when the soul arrives at the head of the Kinvad bridge, the archangels and angels complain of the stench of that soul, and are not able to make up its account and reckoning.
36.6: It remains at the Kinvad bridge and is not able to pass; it experiences much repentance and has no advantage from it.
36.7: If it be necessary for any one to perform the Bareshnûm of the head, and he be able to do it, but does not do it, if he performs the ceremonial ablution of the head a thousand times, it does not become pure from that pollution, and that is the pollution of Nasrust, which is amid the veins and sinews, and the flesh and bones; it does not become pure through any other thing except through the liquid consecrated by the religious formula.
36.8: And as to that person, also, who performs the Bareshnûm for mankind, it is necessary that he be a man, a friend of the soul, a truthful speaker, and an abstainer, because through chastity and modesty (mastûrî) he becomes employed.
36.9: If complaint of any perfidy in him is publicly diffused, in that disgrace (malâmat) it is necessary that the high-priests should dislocate his joints one by one, and it is requisite that they give him as food to the dogs.
36.10: So that by this action they may make a man observe more chastely and continently, that this result (‘hâʓil) of sin may not occur.

37.1: The thirty-seventh subject is this, that, when the days of the guardian spirits come on, it is necessary that all persons, among their own food and devotion, should order and provide the sacred cakes and ceremonial, the sacred feast and benedictions (âfrîngân).
37.2: For these ten days it is incumbent on every one; and those are better which they prepare in their own houses, because the souls go every one to its own house.
37.3: And they should have an ear for them, so that they may prepare the sacred cakes and feast and benedictions.
37.4: Those ten days any one of all the souls—that are in this way in every house where they provide the feast more abundantly—proclaims, as to that master of the house, that family, and the whole who are in that house, and the year's affairs of every kind, that they are very good, and their entry (da‘hl) and coming in are very good.
37.5: And every single good work, on account of which we have spoken of the souls of the departed, becomes just like those we have done for our own souls.
37.6: And, when they pass away from this worldly existence, those souls come again, meeting them, and cause gladness, maintain their courage, and also render them honour in the presence of the creator Hôrmazd, and speak thus: 'These righteous souls did not put us away from remembrance while they were in the world, and we have been satisfied with them; now we are unanimous that thou shouldest provide them equal shares of those good works of ours, and make their souls attain to the position of the righteous.'
37.7: They utter these words, and give those souls confidence, while they make out their account.
37.8: Afterwards, with them, they make the passage of the Kinvad bridge, till they arrive at their own position, and then they return.
37.9: Therefore it is necessary to make an effort, so that they may maintain the guardian spirits properly, and the souls of their fathers and mothers and relations may exist with honour from them.
